column2: He washed his matted hair, he cleaned his gear;
he shook his locks down over his back.
He threw off his filthy things, put on his clean;
he wrapped himself in mantles, tied on the sash.
Gilgameš set the crown on his head —
and on the beauty of Gilgameš princess Ištar lifted her eyes.

Come, Gilgameš. You be the bridegroom.
8	Grant me your fruit — a gift, a granting.
9	You be my husband, and I will be your wife.
10	I will harness for you a chariot of lapis and gold,
11	its wheels of gold, its horns of amber.
12	You will drive in harness great mules that are storms.
13	Enter our house through the fragrance of cedar.
14	When you come into our house,
15	may the splendid doorjamb kiss your feet.
16	May kings, grandees, and princes kneel beneath you;
17	may [all the yi]eld of mountain and lowland come to you as tribute.
18	May your goats drop triplets, your ewes twins;
19	may your foal under its load outgo a mule;
20	may your horse at the chariot be proud in the gallop;
21	may your ox in the yoke have no rival.
[Gilgameš] shaped his mouth to speak,
[say]ing to princess Ištar:

[And if] I take you in marriage —
25	[ ... ] my body and my clothing,
26	[ ... ] my food and my keep?
27	[Would you feed me br]ead fit [for] a god,
28	[pour me ale] fit for a king?
29	[ ... let me] bind(?);
30	[ ... ] let me heap up.
31	[ ... you are wr]apped in a mantle(?) —
32	[what would I get, if] I take you?
33	[You are a hearth that will not ho]ld against ice,
34	a back-door of reed-mat [that will not st]op wind or draught,
35	a palace that crush[es] its own fighting men,
36	an elephant [that shakes off] its housings,
37	pitch that black[ens the hands(?)] of its carrier,
38	a waterskin that soa[ks] its carrier,
39	limestone that [cracks(?)] the stone rampart,
40	a battering-ram that wreck[s] the w[all(?)] of the allied land,
41	a shoe that bites the feet of its owner.
42	Which bridegroom of yours end[u]red for ever?
43	Which brave of yours [ever] went up [to the heavens?]
44	Come, let me tell over [the tal]e of your lovers —
45	of the shoulder [ ... ] his arm:
46	For Dumuzi, the darling of your yo[ut]h,
47	year upon year you decreed the weeping.
48	You loved the speckled roller-bird:
49	you struck him and snapped his wing —
50	now he stands in the woods crying 'My wing!'
51	You loved the lion, perfect in strength:
52	you dug for him pits, seven and seven.
53	You loved the horse, glorious in battle:
54	you decreed for him whip, goad, and lash;
55	you decreed for him a seven-league gallop;
56	you decreed for him churned water for drink;
57	for his mother Silili you decreed perpetual weeping.
58	You loved the shepherd, the herdsman, the master of flocks,
59	[who] al[wa]ys heaped up embers for you,
60	slaughtering kids for you [da]y after day:
61	[you str]uck him and turned him into a wolf —
62	now his own shepherd-boys drive him off,
63	and his own dogs take bites at his thighs.
64	You loved Išullānu, your father's date-gardener,
65	who always brought you baskets of dates,
66	brightening your table day after day.
67	You lifted your eye to him and went to him:
68	'My own Išullānu, let us taste your strength:
69	put out your hand and stroke our sweet place!'
70	Išullānu says to you:
71	'I? What is it you want of me?
72	Has my mother not baked? Have I not eaten,
73	that I should eat the bread of slanders and curses,
74	with esparto-grass my only cover against the cold?'
75	You — you heard this speech of his:
76	you struck him and tu[rned him] into a dwarf(?);
77	you set him down in the middle of [his] gard[en-plot:]
78	no bucket-pole goes up; no [bucket(?)] comes down [ ... ]
79	And me? You will love me, and [use me] like them!
Ištar, when she heard this,
Ištar was enraged, and [went up] to the heavens;
Ištar went we[eping] before An[u] her father;
before Antu her mother her tears kept flowing:

Father — Gilgameš has piled cur[ses] on me!
85	Gilgameš has told over my sl[anders] —
86	my slanders and my curses!
Anu shaped his mouth to speak,
saying to princess Ištar:

Ah, but was it not you who provoked king [Gilga]meš,
90	so that Gilgameš told over your slanders —
91	your slanders and your cu[rses?]
Ištar shaped her mouth to speak,
saying to Anu her father:

Father — give me the Bull of Heaven:
95	let me kill Gilgameš [i]n his own dwelling!
96	And i[f] you do n[ot g]ive me the Bull,
97	I will smash [the underwor]ld(?) down to its dwelling-place;
98	I will se[t ... ] to the world below;
99	I will bring up the [de]ad, and they will eat the li[vi]ng —
100	I will make the dead outnu[mber] the living!
Anu shaped his mouth to [sp]e[ak,]
saying to princess Iš[tar:]
[Ištar shap]ed [her mouth] to speak,
[saying to An]u he[r] father:
B[ef]ore the fury(?) of the Bull [she would ... him.]
Anu [h]eard this speech of Iš[tar,]
[and the l]ead-rope of the Bull he se[t] in her hands,
[and down ... ] Ištar was leading him.
When [he] arrived in [the lan]d of Uruk,
he shrivelled woodland, marsh, and reed-be[d;]
he went down to the river: seven cubits the river dr[op]ped.
At the snorting of the Bull a chasm opened,
and one hundred young men of Uruk kept falling in;
at his second snort a chasm opened,
and two hundred young men of Uruk kept falling in;
at his third snort a chasm opened,
and Enkidu fell in up to [his] wais[t.]
Enkid[u lea]pt up and se[ized] the Bull [b]y [his] horns.
The Bull flung sla[ver] full in his face;
with the thick of his tail [he dropped(?)] his [d]ung.
Enkidu shaped his mouth [to speak,]
saying to Gilga[meš:]

My friend — we made our boa[st in our(?)] cit[y:]
131	how shall we answer the mustered peo[ple?]
132	My friend, I have taken the measure of the Bu[ll's] strength;
133	knowing now his power [and his] bent [ ... ],
134	let me get round [behi]nd(?) the B[ull's] strength:
135	to the rear of the Bull [I will ... ;]
136	I will seize h[im by the thick of his tail;]
137	I will pl[ant my foot on the back(?) of his hock;]
138	in [ ... ]
139	Then [yo]u, like a s[laughterer, br]ave and s[k]illed,
140	between na[pe, ho]rns, and kill-spot(?) thru[st] in your knife!
Enkidu wheeled round to the rear of the Bull;
he seized him by the [thi]ck of his tail;
[he plan]ted his foot o[n the bac]k of h[is] hock;
and Gilgameš, like a s[laughterer], brave and [ski]lled,
between nape, horns, and k[i]ll-spot(?) [thrust in] his knife.
After they had slain the Bull,
they lifted up his heart and set it before Šamaš;
stepping back, they [pr]ostrated themselves before Šamaš,
and the two of them sat down together.
Ištar went up on the wall of Uruk-the-Sheepfold;
she writhed in a stamping dance and shrieked the wo[e-]cry:
That one! Gilgameš — who mocked me — has killed the Bull of Heaven!
Enkidu heard this speech of Ištar:
he tore off the Bull's haunch and flung it in her face.

And you! Could I but reach you, I would use you the same:
157	I would drape his guts along your arms!
Ištar gathered the courtesans, the pleasure-girls, and the harlots;
over the haunch of the Bull she set up a weeping.
Gilgameš summoned the craftsmen, the armorers, all of them;
the craftsmen's sons admire the thickness of his horns:
thirty minas of lapis lazuli their casing;
two minas each their rims;
six measures of oil, the capacity of the pair,
he gave for the anointing of his god Lugalbanda,
and carried the horns in and hung them in his master-bedroom.
In the Euphrates they washed their hands;
they took each other's hand and came riding
through the street of Uruk,
the people of Uruk crowded together gaz[ing] on [them.]
Gilgameš spo[ke] a word to the serving-girls of [his] pala[ce:]

Who is finest among the young men?
173	Who is proudest among the males?

Gilgameš is finest among the young men!
175	[Gilgameš is prou]dest among the males!

[ ... whom] we [k]new in our fury,
177	[ ... i]n his street he has none to disparage him,
178	[ ... the wa]y of [ ... ]
Gilgameš in his palace he[ld] a merrymaking.
The young men lay stretched out, asleep on the couch of night,
and Enkidu, stretched out, was seeing a dream.
Enkidu rose to unravel the dream,
saying to his friend:
